title: Tears of Steel — the complete story

segments.text: The story begins years in the past, with a couple at a crossroads. Thom is a young man whose dream is to go to space and, in his words, to be awesome there. Celia works in robotics, and she has a robot hand.

Celia calls him a jerk. Thom frames the split as two people following their passions, but she pushes him to admit the real reason, and he does: her robot hand freaks him out. He even has nightmares about being chased by giant robotic claws.
And at that exact moment, a voice announces that a robot's memory has been synced and locked. The breakup has just become part of a machine.

The film then lets images carry us through time. In a few sparse lines, someone admits they overheard the couple the night before, and insists it is not their fault, a line that will come back later as a running joke.

In the present, a military operation is about to begin. Thom, visibly nervous, is assured that he is a rockstar. Barley, keeping the clock, gives them about ten minutes, and the soldiers are sent charging out.
Their leader behaves less like a commander and more like a film director. As they finally see her, he coaches Thom like an actor: she is your passion, be tender, be honest, remind her what love is.

Now the plan is clear. They have rebuilt the scene of the breakup, and they are going to shoot it again. Action. A technician confirms that a memory overwrite is in progress, while an actress repeats Celia's first line and Thom recites his old words.
Enemies are two minutes out. Speed it up, Thom, the director shouts, adding an operatic vivacissimo.
With that confession the stakes are out in the open. The woman he left is the one destroying the world. The take falls apart, someone yells abort, the director yells cut, and everyone screams.
Then Celia speaks for herself. He broke her heart. He forgot her on Earth. She should just crush him. Her war on the world was heartbreak all along.

Thom, who has run from this conversation for years, finally says he is sorry, and means it. The director, still in film mode, calls it a good ad-lib, and the running gag returns: not my fault, this time.
They are out of time. The battle reaches its peak, the overwrite reaches ninety percent, and a soldier begs the captain to abort.

The overwrite completes. A story that began with a man running from a robot hand ends with him accepting that people, like worlds, can change. And as the dust settles, the final verdict is a classic understatement: there is a lesson in all this, and it could have gone worse.
